items.title: Javon Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 3, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Delfeayo was someone I went to college with

ctx.x: There was a week, I guess it was around the end of March, where it seemed like every other day one of our influential musicians, we were reading obituaries. And it was very sad and I wondered if you have lost any close musician friends?

Several. Jimmy Heath was a very close friend and mentor. Jimmy passed. Jimmy Cobb was a very close friend and mentor. He just passed recently. McCoy Tyner was someone I had been working with over the last two, three years, he passed. Wallace Roney, who was a bandmate and good friend and someone I learned an immense amount from, he passed. Musicians in Denver that I knew have passed, a couple, and obviously the Marsalis family, Delfeayo was someone I went to college with, the passing of his father, you feel…

Yeah somehow I had to correct myself — I knew Bucky Pizzarelli pretty well and he had been to Hamilton many times, and when he passed away I just felt like that’s not fair somehow, that this took him down even though he was in poor health. And I had to stop myself and say it’s not fair for anybody that’s losing — it’s not just musicians it’s across the board as you had said.

items.title: Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2010
items.q: I represented Colorado, me and another person, and Delfayo Marsalis represented Louisiana. Well when I met him, the first thing I said was, “I want to meet your brother.”

ctx.x: I was in McDonald’s All American Band, a high school all-American band, which takes two students — I don’t know if it exists anymore — but it takes two students from each state in the United States. I represented Colorado, me and another person, and Delfayo Marsalis represented Louisiana. Well when I met him, the first thing I said was, “I want to meet your brother.” We were in New York doing the Macy’s Day parade. And so I remember afterwards, and the first thing I go up to him and I said, “I want to play with…

Really interesting. And it makes me think about earlier you had said, referring to Art Blakey and Elvin Jones, when they passed that there was a short of a signal to shift in jazz some, but you found a mentor and hung with that guy and it led to what you were hoping for. I mean the mentorship thing is not what it used to be, at least in talking to these fellows from the thirties and the forties it seems like.
